Russian Chemicals Sector Rebounds After 2021 Credit Crunch Fallout

In the aftermath of the 2021 financial crisis that swept Russia’s chemicals industry, companies are reflecting on the challenges that gripped the sector during the abrupt credit freeze that year. While conditions in the industry have since stabilized, the impact of the crisis continues to shape strategy and capital allocation for major players.

The crisis began in the first quarter of 2021 when a sudden tightening of credit markets left chemicals producers unable to refinance short-term debt or access working capital. Triggered by a combination of global market volatility, tightening monetary policy, and domestic regulatory uncertainty, the situation saw bond yields spike and credit lines withdrawn nearly overnight.

Sibur Holding PAO, Russia’s largest integrated petrochemicals company, was among those affected. In a statement at the time, the company acknowledged “unprecedented liquidity constraints” and said the disruption had forced it to postpone certain expansion projects and renegotiate supplier contracts. Other leading firms, including the KrasChem Group and UralPolymers, faced similar pressures.

Industry-wide, production volumes dropped sharply as companies scaled back output to conserve cash. According to the Russian Union of Chemical Producers, output across the sector fell by 14% in the three months following the onset of the crisis. “It was a perfect storm for our industry,” said Alexei Morozov, the union’s executive director. “With banks unwilling to lend and foreign investors cautious, even the strongest companies faced tough choices.”

The crisis also saw several mid-sized producers default on their obligations, prompting the government to step in with a short-term liquidity facility amounting to 70 billion rubles. This intervention was credited with preventing a wider cascade of bankruptcies. “State support was critical,” said Olga Petrovna, chief analyst at FinInvest Advisory. “Without it, the contraction could have been much deeper.”

Exporters were particularly hard-hit, as global demand for key products such as fertilizers and plastics softened during the period. The collapse in export revenues squeezed margins and forced firms to focus on domestic markets, where demand remained subdued.

Looking back, Sibur Holding PAO and its peers have since rebuilt their financial positions and resumed growth plans, but executives remain wary. “We learned important lessons about risk management and the importance of diversified funding sources,” said a Sibur spokesperson. “The experience of 2021 has made the sector more resilient for the future.”
